column5: master, servant, camels, goods in hand
column6: Abraham's servant takes his master's camels, with “all the good things of his master” in his hand; the verse supplies a concrete owner-animal-servant tableau for the commentary's property and domestication image.

column5: a servant speaks for his master
column6: The speaker identifies himself as Abraham's servant, a close narrative counterpart to the owned person speaking in the first person after the commentary's shift to “we worship you.”

column5: master's livestock, servants, camels, donkeys
column6: The servant lists his master's wealth as animals, male and female servants, and camels and donkeys, making the commentary's linked possessions socially concrete.

column5: Joseph, Egyptian master, house, all in hand
column6: Joseph serves the Egyptian official, is set over his house, and receives everything the master owns into his hand; this is the biblical Joseph-household setting behind the commentary's human rab/master scene.

column5: master's wife commands Joseph
column6: The Egyptian master's wife orders Joseph to lie with her, the immediate biblical scene corresponding to the commentary's Joseph speaking to the woman in his Egyptian master's house.

column5: my master, house, withheld possession
column6: Joseph calls the Egyptian “my master” and describes his control over the house and its goods, giving a precise human-master use alongside the commentary's discussion of rabbi as an owner.

column5: Arabic ع ب د (source labels B001-B006), Hebrew עבד
column6: Egyptians force Israelites into harsh service; the Hebrew verb is from עבד, a genuine cognate of the commentary's Arabic ع ب د, and its context preserves the coerced labor side of the root.

column5: enslaved people and divine judgment
column6: God says that the nation whom Abraham's descendants serve will be judged; it joins Israel's forced service to judgment, the two poles carried by the commentary's slave language and Day of dīn.

column5: release my son to serve me
column6: God tells Pharaoh to release Israel, called God's son, “that he may serve me”; Hebrew תעבדני shares the ʿbd root with naʿbudu and turns release from Pharaoh into service of God.

column5: Israel belongs to God, not sale as slaves
column6: Because Israelites are God's servants brought from Egypt, they may not be sold in a slave sale; it qualifies the owner-slave analogy by denying an Israelite human master an absolute claim.

column5: do not rule ruthlessly over a servant
column6: The law prohibits ruthless rule over an impoverished Israelite servant and requires fear of God, placing a divine limit on the domination developed in the commentary.

column5: “My servants” and deliverance from Egypt
column6: God twice calls Israelites “my servants”; the verse makes divine ownership the reason they are not ultimately servants of human owners.

column5: slaves as inherited possession
column6: The law permits inherited, permanent possession of foreign slaves, a stark legal counterpart to the commentary's technical treatment of a mamlūk as property.

column5: slave described as master's money
column6: The assault law calls the slave the master's “money”; it directly witnesses the property vocabulary that the commentary places inside the master-slave relation.

column5: one creator of master and servant
column6: Job grounds a servant's right to a hearing in the fact that the same maker formed both master and servant in the womb; it answers creation-based ownership with creation-based equality.

column5: ox knows owner, donkey its master's manger
column6: The ox recognizes its owner and the donkey its master's feeding-place, while Israel does not know; animal ownership becomes a rebuke about recognizing and obeying the divine master.

column5: trained heifer, fair neck, yoke
column6: Hosea depicts Ephraim as a trained heifer whose neck will be yoked for plowing, a close animal image for the commentary's domestication, submission, and forced labor.

column5: wild ox refuses service and manger
column6: God asks whether the wild ox will consent to serve a human or lodge by the manger; its refusal marks the limit of human animal mastery that the commentary depicts as divinely granted.

column5: human dominion over living creatures
column6: The creation command tells humankind to subdue the earth and rule the animals, providing a creation account of the animal authority and use developed through the tamed camel and livestock.

column5: animals placed into human hand
column6: After the flood, every animal is given into human hands; the phrase makes ownership/control of creatures a concrete parallel to the commentary's hand-held property and subdued animals.

column5: donkey's burden and slave's work
column6: Greek Sirach pairs fodder, stick, and burdens for a donkey with bread, discipline, and work for a slave, explicitly yoking animal taming and human subjection as the commentary does.

column5: cattle belong to God
column6: God claims every forest animal and the cattle on a thousand hills; human possession of livestock is set within the creator's prior ownership.

column5: Father who made and acquired you
column6: The song calls God the Father who made, acquired, and established Israel, closely matching the commentary's claim that createdness establishes a prior divine belonging.

column5: created, formed, redeemed, “you are mine”
column6: The creator-former addresses Israel by name and says “you are mine,” an unusually direct biblical formulation of created persons as belonging to God.

column5: formed servant
column6: Israel is told, “you are my servant; I formed you,” joining servanthood to divine formation in the same sequence the commentary makes explicit.

column5: made by God, his people and flock
column6: WLC's ketiv reads that God made us “and not we [ourselves],” while its qere reads “and we are his”; the verse then calls the people his and the flock of his pasture, so both streams need to be kept distinct in this creation-and-belonging parallel.

column5: all lives are God's
column6: God declares that every life, parent and child alike, is God's; the assertion broadens the commentary's ownership image from a household slave to all human persons.

column5: servant honors master, God as master
column6: Malachi argues from a servant's honor for a master to God's claim on Israel's honor, directly using household hierarchy to define proper reverence for God.

column5: servants' eyes to master's hand
column6: The psalm compares Israel's eyes toward God to servants' eyes toward a master's hand and a maid's toward her mistress; it is an exact prayer-image of dependent, direct address.

column5: serve God with gladness
column6: The liturgical command to serve YHWH joyfully gives a cultic form of service that is more than inward feeling, while changing the commentary's stress on extreme abasement.

column5: Arabic إله/الله (source label ء ل ه B001), Hebrew אלהיך
column6: The command to fear and serve “YHWH your God” uses Hebrew אלהיך from the same ʾ-l-h family as the commentary's ilāh/Allah label and directs exclusive service toward that God.

column5: Arabic ع ب د (source labels B001-B006), Hebrew עבד
column6: The prohibition against bowing to or serving other gods uses Hebrew עבד; it gives the cognate root an explicit exclusive-worship setting rather than merely a lexical resemblance.

column5: choose whom to serve; household service
column6: Joshua makes service a confessed choice—“as for me and my house, we will serve YHWH”—which closely parallels the commentary's movement from an existing status to the servant's own voiced assent.

column5: every knee bows to God
column6: God's oath that every knee will bend before him gives a universal biblical scene of bodily submission corresponding to the commentary's claim that all creatures finally come as servants.

column5: prepare and straighten God's highway
column6: The wilderness voice commands a way to be prepared and a highway made straight for God, the nearest biblical counterpart to the commentary's trodden, made-level road.

column5: valleys raised, mountains lowered, rough ground level
column6: The next verse specifies the leveling and smoothing of the road, adding the physical process of subduing terrain rather than only the abstract image of a path.

column5: level ground for Israel's safe walking
column6: Baruch says God commands mountains lowered and valleys filled so Israel may walk safely on level ground, a Jewish expansion of Isaiah's road image into divinely prepared passage.

column5: leveling and smoothing the way
column6: Luke's Isaian quotation retains valleys filled, mountains lowered, and rough places made smooth; it carries the commentary's rendered-road image into the Gospel's preparation for God's coming.

column5: prepare the Lord's way, make paths straight
column6: Mark applies the wilderness-road summons to John's proclamation, making the straightened path a concrete Gospel preparation for the Lord rather than a bare travel image.

column5: yoke of heaven and commandments
column6: Rabbi Joshua ben Korha explains the order of the Shema as first accepting the yoke of the kingdom of heaven and then the yoke of commandments; this gives a Jewish liturgical reading of willingly assumed divine obedience.

column5: servants serving without reward
column6: Antigonus instructs disciples to serve the master without serving for reward and to keep the fear of heaven; it probes how divine service can be freely offered rather than merely compelled.

column5: ear piercing and servants of God
column6: The Talmud explains the permanently pierced Hebrew servant through the Sinai claim that Israel belongs to God, criticizing one who acquires a human master; it is a direct Jewish limit on human lordship.

column5: all animal kinds are tamed
column6: James says every kind of beast, bird, reptile, and sea creature is tamed by humanity, a precise New Testament counterpart to the commentary's language of animal domestication.

column5: the tongue cannot be tamed
column6: The immediately following contrast says no human can tame the tongue; it gives the tamed-animal figure a moral reversal in which the human speaker remains resistant to mastery.

column5: worship and serve God alone
column6: Jesus answers temptation with worship of and service to God alone, a direct Gospel formulation of the exclusive “you we worship” relation.

column5: no one can serve two masters
column6: The maxim about serving God or Mammon makes divided mastership impossible, a close counterpart to the commentary's restriction on treating people or possessions as rival lords.

column5: calling Lord requires obedience
column6: Jesus asks why people call him “Lord, Lord” but do not do what he says; the verse explicitly joins the master's title to obedience, not to verbal address alone.

column5: servant returns from plowing or shepherding
column6: Jesus' household example assumes a servant who comes in from field work and still prepares the master's meal, preserving the literal labor-and-master scene that underlies the commentary's slave image.

column5: servants have done only their duty
column6: After doing all commanded, disciples are to call themselves servants who have only done their duty; it supplies a Christian idiom of obedience and lowly self-description.

column5: master serves watchful servants
column6: The returning master dresses for service, seats his servants, and serves them; this deliberately reverses the commentary's one-way household hierarchy and its claim that the master does not lower himself.

column5: “Teacher and Lord”
column6: Jesus accepts the disciples' titles “Teacher” and “Lord,” giving the human speech of lordship in the commentary an explicit Gospel parallel before the following reversal.

column5: Lord washes servants' feet
column6: The one called Lord and Teacher washes disciples' feet and makes it exemplary; the action directly counters the commentary's asymmetry in which humiliation belongs only to the servant.

column5: Gentile rulers lord it over others
column6: Jesus names dominating rule as the practice of Gentile rulers, making human lordship a social pattern that his teaching will explicitly reject.

column5: greatness becomes service
column6: The next verse reverses status: whoever wants greatness must become the others' servant, changing the master-slave scale from ownership to service.

column5: Son of Man serves and gives ransom
column6: The Son of Man comes not to be served but to serve and give his life as a ransom, a concentrated counter-scene to a master who only receives service.

column5: Christ in God's form
column6: The hymn begins with Christ in God's form, establishing the high status whose subsequent self-emptying makes its relation to the commentary's unlowered owner deliberate rather than generic humility.

column5: form of a slave
column6: Christ takes the form of a slave; the verse turns the commentary's owned and humbled slave role into the role voluntarily assumed by the exalted figure.

column5: humbled obedience to death
column6: The hymn explicitly says he humbled himself and became obedient unto death, matching the commentary's association of worship/service with abasement while reversing who undergoes it.

column5: God highly exalts the humbled one
column6: God's exaltation follows the slave-form and humbling, giving the commentary's secondary movement from lowliness to honor a markedly different Christian sequence.

column5: every knee bends at Jesus' name
column6: The universal bending of knees echoes the commentary's eschatological servanthood, but directs it in the hymn's Christological pattern.

column5: every tongue confesses Jesus as Lord
column6: The final confession calls Jesus “Lord” to the Father's glory, pairing the master's title, universal confession, and worship after the servant-form reversal.

column5: slaves of the one obeyed
column6: Paul states that a person becomes a slave of the one obeyed, whether sin leading to death or obedience leading to righteousness; it closely binds slavery to obedience as the commentary's dīn discussion does.

column5: freed from sin, enslaved to God
column6: Paul calls believers both freed from sin and enslaved to God, a consciously paradoxical account of divine belonging and moral freedom.

column5: slave as Lord's freedperson, free as Christ's slave
column6: Paul reverses ordinary social labels: the enslaved called in the Lord is free, while the free person is Christ's slave; it sharply reframes the commentary's fixed owner-slave status.

column5: bought at a price; do not become human slaves
column6: Because believers were bought at a price, Paul warns them not to become slaves of humans; divine purchase becomes an argument against human mastery.

column5: no longer slave but child and heir
column6: The believer is no longer a slave but a child and heir through God, changing the household relation from permanent servitude to filial inheritance.

column5: not slavery to fear but adoption
column6: Paul contrasts a spirit of slavery leading to fear with adoption that cries “Abba, Father,” offering a different mode of direct address and belonging from the commentary's servile abasement.

column5: earthly masters share a Master in heaven
column6: Christian masters must stop threatening because their own and their slaves' Master is in heaven and shows no partiality; the verse limits human ownership from above.

column5: God made the world and is Lord of heaven and earth
column6: Paul calls the creator Lord of heaven and earth, a New Testament statement of comprehensive divine sovereignty over the worlds named in the commentary.

column5: God is not served as needing anything
column6: God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything, because he gives life and breath to all; it closely supports the commentary's insistence that the true owner lacks no helper and is not reduced by need.

column5: bought with a price and glorify God
column6: Believers are said to have been bought at a price and therefore to glorify God bodily, joining ownership language to a lived act of worship.

column5: another person's household servant
column6: A believer is called another's household servant who stands or falls before his own Lord; the verse makes mastership a reason not to usurp judgment over someone else's servant.

column5: master entrusts property to servants
column6: The parable begins with a man entrusting his own property to his servants, preserving the master-property-servant relation that the commentary treats as a single image.

column5: master returns to settle accounts
column6: The servants' master returns after a long time and settles accounts with them, a literal parabolic meeting of ownership, service, and the reckoning associated with the Day of dīn.

column5: father restores the returning son with honor
column6: The father answers the returning son's household shame with robe, ring, and sandals, making the master's house a place of restorative honor rather than the fixed abasement expected in the commentary.

column5: fear, glory, judgment, worship the creator
column6: The angel announces judgment and commands worship of the maker of heaven, earth, sea, and springs, bringing creator-ownership and Day-of-judgment worship together.

column5: all God's servants praise him
column6: A heavenly voice calls all God's servants, great and small, to praise him; it provides a direct apocalyptic equivalent to praise voiced by those who belong to God.

column5: fellow servant; worship God
column6: The angel refuses John's prostration, identifies as a fellow servant, and commands worship of God; it sharply distinguishes servanthood from receiving worship.

column5: God's servants serve in the final city
column6: In the city of God's throne and the Lamb's throne, the servants will serve him; the final setting gives an eschatological counterpart to universal divine service.

column5: Moses as servant in God's whole house
column6: Moses is faithful as a servant in all God's house, preserving the commentary's house/master/servant relation in an explicitly theological household.

column5: Christ as Son over God's house
column6: The contrast makes Christ Son over God's house and the believers that house, distinguishing sonship and household membership from slave status.

column5: third-person shepherd narration turns to “you”
column6: Psalm 23 moves from “he” as the shepherd who leads in verses 1-3 to direct “you” in verse 4; its exact pronoun turn offers a literary analogue to the commentary's movement from third-person praise to second-person address, though its figure is shepherd and flock.

column5: Arabic د ي ن (source labels B001, B004), Aramaic דינא
column6: Daniel's Aramaic heavenly court says that the dīn sat and books were opened; the cognate juridical word keeps the judgment sense of “Day of dīn” beside the commentary's developed obedience and ownership senses.

column5: Arabic م ل ك (source label B002), Hebrew מלך
column6: Isaiah sees YHWH as “the King”; Hebrew מלך shares the m-l-k root with the commentary's Mālik label, while the verse contributes royal sovereignty rather than treating the Hebrew word as a property term.

column5: prepare the way through Torah study
column6: The Community Rule applies Isaiah's wilderness-way language to a separated group preparing God's way by studying and doing Torah, an interpretive conversion of road-making into disciplined obedience.

column5: yoke of Torah releases other yokes
column6: The mishnah says accepting the yoke of Torah removes the yoke of government and worldly burdens; it develops divine submission as release from rival subjections.

column5: servant treated as brother
column6: After its donkey-and-slave discipline imagery, Sirach tells the owner to treat a servant as a brother; the nearby ethical reversal complicates a reading of the owned person as only property.

column5: slave and son in the household
column6: Jesus says a slave does not remain in the household forever but the son does; it uses the house image to contrast slave impermanence with filial permanence.

column5: no longer servants but friends
column6: Jesus no longer calls disciples servants because a servant does not know the master's affairs, but friends; intimate disclosure revises the distance assumed by the master-property model.

column5: no longer a slave but a beloved brother
column6: Paul asks that Onesimus be received no longer merely as a slave but as a beloved brother in the Lord, an explicit Christian re-description of an owned person's relation.

column5: master and slave hope in the same God
column6: The Didache forbids bitter commands to male or female slaves because both slave and master hope in the same God; it applies common divine lordship to household conduct.

column5: creation, animal rule, slavery after sin
column6: Augustine argues that the created order gives humans rule over irrational creatures, while human slavery is bound to sin; this Christian reading separates animal dominion from a natural right to own persons.

column4: Gregory of Nyssa, Homilies on Ecclesiastes 4
column5: buying humans made in God's image
column6: Gregory's homily on Ecclesiastes 2:7 attacks the purchase of human beings by appealing to their divine image and created freedom, a pointed patristic challenge to calling a person property.

column5: returning son asks to be a hired servant
column6: The returning son proposes admission to his father's house as a hired servant; paired with the father's response in verse 22, it makes the commentary's servant-at-the-master's-house image a precise Gospel encounter.

column5: house, servants, ox, donkey, every possession
column6: The anti-coveting command gathers a neighbor's house, male and female servants, ox, donkey, and other possessions into one household inventory, closely matching the commentary's owner-house-animal-slave tableau.

column5: servant chooses master, wife, children, household
column6: The Hebrew servant says that he loves his master, wife, and children and will not go free; this gives a legal counter-case in which continued belonging is explicitly voiced as a choice.

column5: doorpost, pierced ear, permanent service
column6: The master brings the willing servant to the doorpost and pierces his ear for lifelong service, a concrete ritualization of ownership and enduring service in the master's house.

column5: Sabbath rest for ox, donkey, servant
column6: The Sabbath command joins the ox and donkey to the child of the slave woman and resident alien in receiving rest, placing a divine limit on the labor imposed upon both working animals and dependent people.

column5: servant rests “as you do”
column6: The Decalogue's Sabbath law requires the male and female servant to rest as the owner rests; it turns the master-slave relation into an equality of rest before God.

column5: Israel released from serving Egypt
column6: When Israel has gone, Egypt describes the loss as letting them go “from serving us”; the phrasing gives the Pharaoh-Israel bondage in the commentary a direct narrative counterpart.

column5: human master bounded by sin against God
column6: Joseph says his master has withheld nothing but his wife, yet refuses because the act would be a sin against God; the human householder's wide control is subordinated to a higher Lord.

column5: direct “I am your servant”; bonds loosed
column6: The psalmist directly calls himself God's servant and son of God's maidservant, then says God has loosed his bonds; it keeps divine servanthood and liberation together in one prayer.

column5: bow, kneel, maker
column6: The congregation is summoned to bow down and kneel before YHWH its maker, a close liturgical image of embodied abasement before the creator.

column5: people of pasture, flock of God's hand
column6: The worshippers are God's people and the flock of his hand; it combines animal dependence, the owner's hand, and collective divine belonging.

column5: life of animals and humans in God's hand
column6: Job places the life of every living creature and the breath of all humanity in God's hand, extending the commentary's hand-held possession figure beyond livestock to all life.

column5: everything under heaven belongs to God
column6: God asks who could give first so that God owed repayment, because all under heaven is God's; it joins universal possession to divine non-dependence.

column5: earth and inhabitants belong to YHWH
column6: The psalm's opening ownership formula gives YHWH the earth, its fullness, the world, and its inhabitants, an explicit scriptural horizon for “Lord of the worlds.”

column5: all comes from God; gifts returned
column6: David's praise says all things come from God and that Israel gives only what is already God's; it makes praise an acknowledgment that human possessions remain received goods.

column5: wise servant shares a son's inheritance
column6: A prudent servant rules over a shameful son and shares the inheritance with the brothers, overturning a fixed hierarchy of owner, household, and slave.

column5: one guarding a master is honored
column6: Proverbs says the one who keeps or attends to a master will be honored, a compact wisdom parallel to the commentary's secondary possibility that service and honor meet.

column5: exalted servant
column6: God's servant is described as raised, lifted up, and greatly exalted, supplying a scriptural servant-and-honor trajectory beside the commentary's muʿabbad sense.

column5: fasting that breaks every yoke
column6: The fast God chooses loosens bonds, frees the oppressed, and breaks every yoke; it makes worship answer human subjugation by liberation rather than by extending it.

column5: Father, potter, clay, work of hands
column6: The prayer calls God Father and potter and the people clay made by God's hand, a creation-and-forming image for dependence that does not reduce them to household property.

column5: clay in potter's hand, house of Israel
column6: God compares the house of Israel to clay in a potter's hand, a particularly close biblical image for formed material held under a maker's authority.

column5: refusal to serve gods or worship the image
column6: The Judean servants tell the king that they will neither serve his gods nor worship his golden image, a concrete refusal of a ruler's imposed cultic mastery.

column5: judge, lawgiver, king
column6: YHWH is named Israel's judge, lawgiver, and king; the verse gathers the judicial and sovereign dimensions that meet in the commentary's Mālik of the Day of dīn.

column5: God brings every deed into judgment
column6: The closing maxim says God will bring every deed, hidden or open, into judgment, providing an explicit Hebrew Bible counterpart to the reckoning implied by Day of dīn.

column5: humble king riding a donkey
column6: Zion's king comes righteous and victorious yet humble, mounted on a donkey; the royal figure unites authority, lowliness, and a domesticated animal in a configuration that reverses the commentary's unlowered master.

column5: make straight paths for feet
column6: Hebrews commands straight paths for the feet so that the lame may be healed rather than put out of joint, turning the made-level road into a communal moral action.

column5: gentle king mounted on donkey
column6: Matthew presents the king as gentle and mounted on a donkey, carrying Zechariah's master-humility-and-domesticated-animal figure into the Gospel entry scene.

column5: servant falls before master over debt
column6: The servant falls down before his master and begs for patience over the debt, giving a literal scene of servile prostration, ownership, and reckoning.

column5: master releases servant and forgives debt
column6: The master is moved with compassion, releases the servant, and cancels the debt; this masterly authority is expressed through liberation rather than permanent subjection.

column5: direct prayer to creator as Sovereign Master
column6: The community addresses God as despota, the Sovereign Master who made heaven, earth, sea, and all in them; it joins direct address, mastery, and creation in one prayer.

column5: Cornelius falls at a human's feet
column6: Cornelius falls at Peter's feet and prostrates before him, staging the very transfer of honor to a human figure that the commentary's limit on human lords excludes.

column5: Peter refuses human prostration
column6: Peter raises Cornelius and says that he too is human, turning the preceding act into an explicit rejection of worshipful elevation of a person.

column5: bodies offered as living sacrifice and worship
column6: Paul calls the presentation of embodied life to God a living sacrifice and rational worship, giving worship a concrete, whole-person form beyond a merely verbal confession.

column5: slaves serve the Lord Christ
column6: In an instruction to household slaves, Paul says that the service ultimately rendered is to the Lord Christ and promises an inheritance, placing earthly service under a different master and reward.

column5: free people as slaves of God
column6: Believers are to live as free people while also as God's slaves; the deliberate pairing gives a Christian reversal of the commentary's ordinary contrast between freedom and owned status.

column5: acceptable worship with reverence and awe
column6: The community is to offer acceptable worship to God with reverence and awe because it receives an unshakable kingdom, a liturgical form of humble service before sovereignty.

column5: all appear before Christ's judgment seat
column6: All people must appear before Christ's judgment seat to receive according to their deeds, an individual accounting scene for the Day of dīn dimension.

column5: a fixed day for judging the world
column6: Paul says God has fixed a day on which he will judge the world in righteousness, making the day-and-judgment element explicit in the same speech that calls God creator and Lord.

column5: only Sovereign, King of kings, Lord of lords
column6: The doxology calls God the only Sovereign and the King of kings and Lord of lords, a compact New Testament royal-master formulation beside Mālik.

column5: direct praise to the creator
column6: The heavenly elders say directly, “You are worthy,” because God created all things by his will; it closely joins praise, direct address, and creation-based sovereignty.

column5: Sovereign Lord asked to judge
column6: The martyrs address God as Sovereign Lord and ask when God will judge, bringing master-language and the delayed final judgment into a single direct prayer.

column5: acquiring a Hebrew servant acquires a master
column6: The Talmud's maxim that one who acquires a Hebrew servant acquires a master develops Torah's service law into a reversal: the owner must meet the servant's needs so fully that mastery is ethically displaced.

column5: slaves serve for God's glory and better freedom
column6: Ignatius tells enslaved Christians to serve more diligently for God's glory so that they may receive a better freedom from God, preserving the tension between social servitude and divine freedom.
